title: Don Redman, the unsung hero
summary: Redman's credit went to Benny Goodman; Barefield worked with him again around 1958 with Pearl Bailey. He says Redman could play any instrument, helped the Mills Brothers, and was barely mentioned at his funeral.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Well, you know, they always talk about how, you know, he -- his band never really got the acclaim that it should have gotten, and then of course, at first, when he wrote for Benny Goodman, Benny Goodman's band got --

Right. Yeah, because he -- all of the things that he recorded in the '20s, Benny Goodman came back and got famous on them in the '30s. Don Redmon was another great musician. In fact, I worked with him -- what year? Oh, even after I recorded with him in -- in the late '30s or first of the '40s, whatever it was, I came back with him again, with Pearl Bailey, when he was conducting for Pearl Bailey. I forget what year -- years those were.
This was the late '50s, wasn't it?

Something like that. And we played -- he had a band, a nice, a marvelous band with Pearl Bailey and Louie Belson on drums, and he had Sam Taylor and me and Sammy Most and George Dorsey, and we played around. But Don was a very unsung hero of music. I think he was one of the greatest, you know, all around musicians because he could play any instrument in the orchestra, you know. He played -- and when he was with the Cottonpickers, whoever was missing, he would just sit down and play the book, trumpet, trombone, piano, guitar; anything that he had to play, he played.
Well, he has been given credit for being, you know, really shaping the whole idea of the big band arrangement.
Right. That's right, uh-huh. And I think he's the one that really got the Mills Brothers off on the right track.
Well, before Don Redmon, before they started to sing with Don Redmon, remember when Don Redmon had that commercial, radio show years -- around 1933-34?
Well, he had a big band and had a radio commercial. I don't know whether it was Camel cigarettes

or somebody, and he had the Mills Brothers with him. Before they met Don, they were singing wrong harmonies and everything, and after that they really got their ideas straightened out by just being, working with Don and happening to -- but it's a shame that, when he died, he didn't -- they didn't even mention his name in the funeral.
They had his funeral over on 72nd at Walter B. Cookman. The place was too small for the people in the first place, and he was a Jehovah's Witness.
And they didn't -- they just talked about our dear brother and that was all. They didn't mention none of his accomplishments or anything.
